LifePod Launch

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
University of Stellenbosch Medical students are turning the tide on South Africa's organ donation crisis.

Unique Selling Point:
Over 5000 people across South Africa are waiting for lifesaving organ transplants. It can take years to reach the top of the waiting list. But, a group of university medical students is determined to improve the rate of transplantations in South Africa.



Summary:
Jonty Wright is a fifth year Stellenbosch University medical student who met Lynette Stuurman at the Stellenbosch University canteen. She’s been waiting for a kidney transplant for years, and has dialysis several times a week. Her story moved Jonty, and sparked his interest in this field.

Together with fellow students, they created “Lifepod” – South Africa’s first official dedicated transplant ICU at Tygerberg Hospital. After brain death, and consent from family members, potential donors can be moved to this new ICU instead of occupying trauma unit beds.

Last year, these students competed in Ironman 70.3 to raise awareness and funds, and raised R400,000 through crowdfunding campaigns. They conceptualized “LifePod” with Tygerberg doctors and lecturers. And designed and wrote all operational policies.
LifePod could save up 100 lives annually, and turn the tide on South Africa’s organ donation crisis.


Further information:
A transplant surgeon will also do an interview with us, about the need for these units, and the extensive waiting lists for life saving organ transplant operations.

Script:


VO 1 Some days, Lynette Stuurman wishes she could turn back the clock.

VO 2 Her childhood was a happy, healthy one.

VO 3 There were no signs of the genetic disorder she’d inherited from her father - a kidney disease that would ultimately claim his life, and later that of Lynette’s sibling too.

UPSOUND Lynette Stuurman: My half sister, she passed away in July 2019, and then I decided to have myself tested. They took blood and then the day afterwards I got a call, “Lynette I need to see you”. And I knew Ok that’s not good news.

VO 4 Lynette was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease. She’s now on dialysis three times a week, and is on the transplant waiting list.

UPSOUND Lynette Stuurman / Dialysis patient: If you are lucky you get a kidney within ten, fifteen years. Many of us aren’t that lucky, so we don’t live that long.

FADE TO BLACK

NATSOUND

VO 5 Jonty Wright and Naazim Nagdee are leading this group of Stellenbosch University medical students on a mission.

VO 6 They may look more like a professional cleaning squad, than our future doctors, but already they are making a difference.

VO 7 During their training at Tygerberg Hospital, they realised the shortage of ICU beds was slowing down the organ donation process. The problem they were told…

UPSOUND Jonty Wright / Stellenbosch University Medical Student: We just don’t have space, right, we’d love to, but there’s no space.

VO 8 It was then that their idea was born – to create a space where a braindead donor can be kept to keep their organs alive.

UPSOUND Jonty Wright: What would it take for us to do a formal room at Tygerberg where we can send these patients and enable this life saving process to happen. Picture a braindead donor and we’ve got consent, they now need to be stored in ICU level conditions for 36 hours, and ICU bed space is probably one of the most scarce medical resources in our country and we often don’t refer them cos a child with spinal injury needs it, and rightly so. So, we don’t have the bed space to keep these donors and that’s why we started the Lifepod.

VO 9 Jonty and Naazim began raising awareness and money through their already established non-profit organisation Save7.

LINK: Imagine saving seven lives with just one decision. That’s the power of organ donation. And this group of future doctors is making it easier for that life saving decision to be made.

UPSOUND Jonty Wright: Each and every one of us can save up to seven lives after we pass on, simply by asking our families to donate our life saving organs right. So, I’ve got seven life saving organs within me right now and so do you, right. We’ve got two lungs, a heart, two kidneys, you can also donate your small intestine. Funnily enough you can actually donate your tissue as well, so I can give somebody their sight back by donating my corneas, skin, bone. All recyclable parts basically.

VO 10 Naazim is the vice president and co-founder of Save7.

UPSOUND Naazim Nagdee / Stellenbosch University Medica Student: Save7 basically exists to raise awareness about the people waiting for organs. We ultimately here for people. There’s solutions out there. There’s just no one to pull it forward, no one to push it forward.

VO 11 But, it’s what Naazim, Jonty and their fellow students are now doing. Putting their time and elbow grease into preparing the LifePod, South Africa’s first official organ donor unit, which opens next month.

VO 12 Jonty has wanted to be a doctor..since he was a boy. His mother suffered from chronic migraines, and he saw how debilitating they were.

UPSOUND Jonty Wright: She was obviously in pain a lot and being able to see what a doctor can do, with even just a little bit of medical insight, and the impact it had on her, like being able to go out instead of sit in a dark room in bed all day. That had an impact on me.

VO 13 Now, as a fifth year medical student he’s realised he can make a difference in the organ donor field before even qualifying as a doctor.

UPSOUND Jonty Wright: Save7 was started at the end of my first year. I think if the purpose of studying medicine is to learn how to save lives, you don’t have to wait to do it.

VO 14 In 1967, Dr Christiaan Barnard made history with the world’s first human heart transplant at Groote Schuur hospital in Cape Town. But, today South Africa faces a severe organ donor crisis.
LINK: Just 0,2% of the population is registered as organ donors. That’s one of the lowest rates in the world…and that’s led to a critical shortage.

VO 15 Tygerberg Hospital is South Africa’s second largest and a training ground for Stellenbosch medical students. Its dialysis unit is packed with patients awaiting kidney transplants.

VO 16 Dialysis is a treatment that does the kidneys’ job when they fail.
It cleans the blood artificially—but takes so much time, many patients, like Lynette have to stop working.

UPSOUND Lynette Stuurman: After dialysis I am so dizzy and when I get home, I can’t do anything, I need to go lie down. And that’s how most of my day is spent which is not easy, it’s quite tough. So ja, all in all, it’s been a very rough, rough journey.

LINK: In South Africa, over five thousand people are waiting for life saving transplants, with some kidney patients waiting over twenty years.

UPSOUND Jonty Wright: We’re losing up to sixty viable organs each and every week instead of giving them to the people who need them the most, so that they can go on living. And we’re choosing to donate them to the grave. The issue that we’re focussing on at the moment though is that even if we had consent from everybody, we don’t have the bed space to put donors in, to ensure they can be kept for the 36 hours necessary before the transplant operation happens.

VO 17 Organ transplant surgeon Professor Elmi Muller believes the Lifepod is an innovative way of addressing South Africa’s organ donor shortage.

UPSOUND Prof Elmi Muller / Stellenbosch University: Health Sciences Dean: Of course, we cannot harvest organs just straight away when somebody is braindead. We need to do some tests on them, we need to be able to screen for infections, and do some tissue typing bloods, those things take a lot of time. And in that time we have to keep the donor stable before we can take the organs out. Now this creates a unique space where we can put patients to use a resource that’s already available in a way that’s innovative and that creates opportunities for driving transplantation.

VO 18 Last year, Jonty took part in the half Iron Man to raise funds for equipment for the Lifepod. And through crowdfunding campaigns, the students managed to raise R400,000.

UPSOUND Naazim Nagdee: We’re hoping to process about one donor per month. Now, that doesn’t seem like a lot, but for perspective, sometimes only one donor is processed every six months. And, so we’re hoping once this unit is up and running it will create a pipeline up to 100 lives a year, and our dialysis unit is full of people that need help.

VO 19 Professor Sa’ad Lahri is especially proud of his students. He teaches them emergency medicine, and advised them throughout the process of setting up the LifePod.

MAC: You’ve obviously mentored a lot of students. What made this group extra special?

UPSOUND Professor Sa’ad Lahri / Head of Emergency Medicine: Stellenbosch University: It’s their drive man and their grit, you know. They faced some obstacles, but they never gave up and they persisted. This was something from the heart, no pun intended.

VO 20 Most importantly, the Lifepod provides a quiet area away from the overcrowding and chaos of an emergency setting.

UPSOUND Prof Sa’ad Lahri: That for me is a huge, huge thing. We can offer that donor and their family dignity.

VO 21 Trained by top doctors, these students are gaining clinical experience in an overburdened environment. But, instead of overwhelming them, it inspires them.

UPSOUND Naazim Nagdee: When you train in that sort of environment, there’s a lot of challenges and you realise that, as a young person, you know, you have the energy to try and solve them.
UPSOUND Jonty Wright: Like the hundred and twenty three people who helped us put this together – who recognised that yes there is a problem, but I am capable of being one part of the solution.

VO 22 For Lynette, the Lifepod means she is one step closer to getting a new, healthy kidney.

UPSOUND Lynette Stuurman: What better gift to give than the gift of life, the gift of hope. There are so many babies that are dying and people are not aware that you know they can make a difference. So that is really something beautiful and worthwhile to do before you should leave this earth.

VO 23 And the good news, these young doctors in the making, aren’t going anywhere.

MAC: Do you see a future for yourself in this country?

UPSOUND Jonty: Definitely ja, I believe we were called to stay. I’m going to stay.
UPSOUND Naazim: This country has given me a lot and all those privileges it’s given me, I have to give back. Definitely, I’m staying.
